summary: The 2D screening label is not_2d_applicable and Studio did not run (simulation status skipped). The gate failed on input validity: a custom experiment needs 1–128 blocks and a power_w object, but the floorplan and power_w are empty. simulation_allowed is false and comparison_valid is false, so the final verdict is that no Studio result exists. The scenario is a custom 2D steady run, so it has no transient trace, yet the paper's observable is transient. The paper reports a measured peak core temperature of 60.7 C for RT-TAS (TEA 66.7 C, BASE 72.9 C) on a physical Nvidia Tegra X1. This is the maximum over 4 CPU cores and the GPU and over time, taken from on-chip sensors under 400 ms periodic vision tasks, 15 W rating, 1.15 C/W chip resistance, fan off, and a 65 C throttle threshold. No Studio temperature exists, so no numerical comparison is made and nothing here claims replication. Qualitatively, the paper suggests that scheduling and task-to-core placement change peak temperature by several degrees. A spatial 2D model could not test this from the published data, because the scheduling mechanisms have no floorplan analog. No bundled EV6/GCC adaptation or pinned Ascend910/ATPlace placement with generated input.flp and input.ptrace was used, so no source commit or placement assumption applies. The paper links are only a publisher DOI, Linux CFS documentation, and the cpuburn page, and none supplies inputs.

No floorplan geometry is published: no block x, y, width or height, no die size, no layout coordinates. Fig. 1 is only a qualitative layout schematic. A block-geometry thermal model cannot be built from the paper alone, and no pinned packet asset supplies it.

The original method is a lumped RC thermal-coupling model identified empirically plus real hardware measurement. It is not a spatial 2D or 3D finite-difference/finite-element solver, so a Studio spatial solver would be a different solver class and results cannot be compared numerically with the paper.

The workload is transient and time-varying: periodic jobs, priority inversions and co-scheduling. The published power data are per-task average CPU/GPU power values (Table 2) with no per-block power time series, so a one-row steady power trace would not reproduce the paper's transient dynamics.

The optimizer (T-WFD task-to-core assignment) and the controller (online co-scheduling with inversion budgets, hardware DVFS throttling at 65 C, CPU frequency 1.7 to 0.5 GHz) are scheduling-level mechanisms with no floorplan or placement analog in a thermal Studio.

Real packaging and cooling are not specified in detail: Tegra X1 package, heat spreader, board, passive heat sink and ambient temperature. Only the aggregate chip thermal resistance of 1.15 C/W (from a Nvidia design guide) is given, with the fan off. Thermal-resistance-matrix coefficients (Table 1) are core-level and not material or geometry parameters.

No 3D stacking or interposer is involved. The Tegra X1 is a monolithic 2D SoC, so 3D and interposer mismatches do not apply. Reliability (MTTF, 1.52x lifetime) and cooling-cost ($15.6 per chip) are derived analytically and are not Studio outputs.
